doc.title: Michael Abene interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Several pieces at once, deadlines and teaching schedule
summary: Abene works on two or three pieces at once and works best near the deadline, citing the seven-trombone piece for the Metropole Orchestra; he teaches four days a week and co-directs the BMI workshop.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Is it easier for you to write when you have less choices to make, instrumentation wise, or when you have this huge possibility of a big band and an orchestra?

It’s a very good question. It’s variable. It all depends. Some pieces fall into place a little easier. It’s hard. Sometimes I’ve had more trouble figuring what to do with a band than I do with a full orchestra. Or vice versa. There’s no set thing for me on it. And I’m generally working on two or three pieces at one time. So like if I run into a road block on one I stop and start working on this. And sometimes something will ring a bell working on this piece for this piece. And I get nervous when I’m only working on one piece at a time.

Yeah. And sometimes — I did this one thing for seven trombones for the Metropole Orchestra in the Netherlands. A wonderful orchestra, it was for a big trombone festival two years ago. And seven trombones plus the full orchestra which is about 70 musicians. So it was kind of a difficult piece. Each trombone player gave me an original and I had to write about an hour’s piece of music locking all these things together. So I’m like sitting on — I know I have a deadline. I work better as the deadline gets closer. You know because if I had a year to write something I would be aah write a note, aah. Next thing I know it’s like three months away, two months, then finally wham, something happens, I start clicking in. It kind of forces me, which some guys can work, like this piece for the Slovenia, not it’s November 20 is the concert, next year. So I know right now there’s no way I’m even thinking about it at this point, and that’s generally because I’m trying to get these other things done. And at some point as it gets closer I have, I know who the strong soloists are, I know all the doubles so I know what I’m looking at and I know the band. So as things get a little closer, maybe two months away or three months away, I’ll start to zero in on it. And you know my teaching at Manhattan School of Music is now up to like four days a week. It started off as one, then it was two, and I’m also — Jim McNeely and I are the music directors at the BMI Jazz Composers Workshop. So I live out of the city so I come into the city four days a week and I try to keep the weekends for writing. So it’s like I’m really — there’s some serious discipline going on. It doesn’t look like it sometimes. ©Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
